o: Count distinct subarrays containing at most k elements divisible by p. With n ≤ 200, there are O(n^2) subarrays, and each can be inspected in O(n), so even O(n^3) fits — but the follow-up asks for O(n^2). Distinctness means identical value sequences count once, e.g. [2] appearing at indices 0, 3, 4 counts once in example 1 (answer 11).
k: n ≤ 200 means enumerating all O(n^2) subarrays with incremental divisibility counting is feasible.
Distinctness can be handled by hashing subarray tuples into a set, or by inserting value sequences into a trie.
Extending a subarray one element at a time lets the divisible-element count be maintained in O(1).

a.n: Brute Force with Hash Set of Tuples
a.i: Fix the left endpoint, extend rightward while maintaining a running count of elements divisible by p; stop early once it exceeds k. Store each subarray as a tuple in a set so duplicates collapse automatically.
s: For each start i, scan j from i to n-1.
Maintain count of nums[t] % p == 0; break when count > k.
a.t: O(n^3) worst case for hashing/copying subarrays — fine for n ≤ 200.
a.sp: O(n^3) stored subarray content in the worst case.

a.i: Insert every valid subarray character-by-character into a trie rooted at each start index. Each trie node created corresponds to a previously-unseen subarray, so counting node creations counts distinct subarrays exactly, with no hashing of full sequences.
s: Create an empty trie root (map from value to child map).
For each start i, walk a pointer from the root, extending with nums[j].
Track the divisible count; break when it exceeds k.
Each time a child key is missing, a new distinct subarray was found — increment the answer.
a.t: O(n^2) — each subarray extends the walk by one step with O(1) trie work.
a.sp: O(n^2) trie nodes in the worst case.

w: Prefer the trie in an interview since it directly answers the O(n^2) follow-up and avoids expensive tuple hashing. Pitfall: breaking too late (must exceed k, not reach it) and forgetting that equal-valued subarrays at different positions count once. Rolling hash is a third option but risks collisions; the trie is deterministic.
